newsitem.title: KENYA: World Bank approves cash for Kenya's power sector.
newsitem.headline: World Bank approves cash for Kenya's power sector.

text.p: The World Bank has approved $125 million in credit to Kenya for rehabilitation of a dilapidated power sector crucial to economic growth, a senior regional World Bank official said on Monday.

Harold Wackman, country director for Kenya and Djibouti, told reporters in Nairobi that the cash would help improve power supply and distribution. Severe shortages in power supply are seen as heavily undermining the manufacturing and business sectors.
"The world bank board has approved $125 million for the power sector," he told reporters at a news conference.

Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem told Reuters at a separate briefing that shortages in power supply, a poor road network, expensive telephones and an inefficient port were some of the major drawbacks in Kenya's campaign for growth.
In April, Kenya Power & Lighting Co (KP&LC) ended seven months of power rationing after heavy rains improved water levels in main supply stations and repair work on others ended.
Three independent power producers are also expected to start supplying the Kenyan national grid in July and the World Bank cash will go towards other KP&LC power-improvement projects.

Kenya's capacity generated oscillates between 570 and 650 megawatts while installed capacity is 784 megawatts. The deficiency is blamed on poor weather, poor maintenance and constant breakdowns. Outages remain despite a rationing end.
Cheserem also urged Kenya's political leaders to solve their problems through dialogue because chaos discouraged investment.

On Thursday, Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi read his speech amid the most chaotic scenes seen in Kenya's parliament chamber. Opposition members of parliament calling for constitutional reforms disrupted his budget speech before a punch-up with MPs of the ruling KANU party.
Mudavadi put repair of infrastructure on top of his agenda.

"The problem is that the politicians have promised so much and delivered so little," Cheserem told Reuters. "There is no investment in a rioters' country. The people are saying, do not involve us in chaotic confrontations. Think about the economy."

Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi told Roman Catholic bishops on Saturday that he was personally not an obstacle to reforms. He said he was concerned about strife that accompanied the clamour for reforms across the world's poorest continent.
Cheserem said that he expected the Kenyan shilling to remain steady against the dollar in the July-December period despite jitters associated with general elections later this year.
"Unless there are real chaos, we don't see a major impact (of the election process) on the currency," Cheserem said.
The shilling traded at a mean of 55.05 versus the dollar on Monday, according to Central Bank of Kenya statistics.
He said there were steady foreign inflows of hard currency from investors in the benchmark 91-day treasury bills and the central bank was holding reserves worth 5.6 months in imports.
Mudavadi forecast gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 4.0 percent in 1997 and Cheserem saw poor infrastructure as the biggest threat to meeting that target.
